verses.note: The first law is almost entirely permission. Obedience in Eden is not the price of life but the shape of trust: the man is asked to take God's word about good and evil rather than decide it for himself.

This is the first food law in Scripture, given to all of Noah's descendants before Israel exists. The Jerusalem council in Acts 15 asked Gentile believers to abstain from blood, which many interpreters connect with this command given to all humanity rather than only to Israel.

God binds himself to require an accounting for human life. Bloodshed is not a private matter between killer and victim's family; it is an offense God himself pursues, which is the ground on which later biblical law treats murder as a wrong against the community and against God.

Christians have long disagreed over what this verse requires of governments. Many find in it the foundation for the state's authority to punish murder, including by death, and connect it with Romans 13:4. Others read it as describing the way bloodshed breeds bloodshed and point to Jesus' words about those who take the sword (Matthew 26:52). Both sides agree that the verse makes human life sacred because of whose image it bears.

The verse describes a man before Sinai in the language of Sinai, which suggests that the law did not introduce a new kind of relationship with God. It gave shape to the same listening obedience that Abraham already practiced.

What Joseph's brothers did was later named a capital crime in Israel's law: “Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death” (Exodus 21:16, see also Deuteronomy 24:7). Joseph's word ‘stolen’ is the law's word.

Leviticus 25 takes the word befarekh from this verse and forbids it among God's people. Israel's law is shaped by its history: what was done to them in Egypt defines what they may not do to one another.

The experience of being a ger shapes Israel's law: Israel must not oppress the foreigner, because it knows how a foreigner feels, having been one in Egypt (Exodus 23:9). Moses lives that experience personally before he gives the law.

‘One law’ binds the native and the foreigner equally. The principle recurs in Leviticus 24:22 and Numbers 15:15-16, and it makes Israel's law a protection for the stranger rather than an instrument of privilege.

The commands rest on a completed act of deliverance. Obedience is the response of the freed, not the price of freedom, and the Reformers took this verse as a key to the right use of the law among the redeemed.

The last command shows that the law aims at the heart. No court could enforce it, so it lays bare the root from which the other offenses grow and anticipates Jesus' teaching that evil acts come from within (Mark 7:21-23).

Some laws of the Torah bind Israel alone, but these bind anyone who lives among God's people. Their inclusion of the foreigner shows that the one altar is not an ethnic privilege but the only legitimate place for anyone in the land to approach God.
The law is given to be taught and lived in a particular land. It is not an abstract code but instruction for a people's life in the place God is giving them.
Every other law in Deuteronomy serves this one. Jesus draws out what is already implied when he says the whole Law and the Prophets hang on it and the command to love one's neighbor (Matthew 22:40).
The commands are a gift given for Israel's good. This is the Old Testament's own answer to the idea that God's law is arbitrary: it is the shape of a life that flourishes.

Which law is written on the heart? Reformed interpreters, following Calvin, hold that it is the same moral law of God, now written inwardly by the Spirit. Lutheran and many Baptist and New Covenant theology interpreters stress that the law of Christ, not the Mosaic code as such, is what believers keep. Jewish interpreters such as David Kimchi (Radak) read it as the same Torah, finally kept. All agree the verse promises inward obedience, not lawlessness.

Joseph's righteousness keeps the law without cruelty. Matthew later has Jesus rebuke those who keep the law's small details and neglect justice, mercy, and faithfulness (23:23) and twice quote Hosea's word that God desires mercy (9:13, 12:7). The first righteous man in the Gospel already lives that way.

The one who says he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them (5:17) begins by fulfilling ‘all righteousness’. Jesus' own obedience comes before any demand he makes of his disciples that their righteousness exceed the scribes' (5:20).

Jesus places himself as the goal of the whole Old Testament, ‘the Law or the Prophets’. The law is neither discarded nor left unchanged: it is brought to what it was always aiming at, in his teaching and in his person.

Jesus does not quote the commandment in order to loosen it but to trace it to its root. The antithesis contrasts not Moses and Jesus but a reading of the law that stops at the outward act and one that reaches the heart.
Jesus claims to state the heart of the law, not to replace it. The Golden Rule is Leviticus 19:18 turned into a practical test: imagine yourself in the other's place and act accordingly.

Jesus has just said that he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (5:17), and the first deed after the sermon puts that into practice: the healed man is sent to obey what Moses commanded. The cure is new; the obedience is the old one.

Jesus answers a question about purity by sending his critics to Scripture: ‘go and learn’. The Law and the Prophets are read by their own priorities, and Hosea supplies the ranking: God desires mercy above sacrifice. This is not the Law set aside but the Law's own aim, the same principle Jesus will call the weightier matters (23:23).

The new wine is the presence of the bridegroom and the kingdom he brings, and it requires new forms. Matthew's ‘both are preserved’, alongside his saying that every scribe trained for the kingdom brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old (13:52), shows his concern that the new not destroy what God gave before. Interpreters differ on how much of the Law's practice continues and how much is fulfilled and ended in Christ, a second-order question this verse opens rather than settles.

The verse treats the law not only as command but as prophecy, a word that looked ahead to its fulfillment. That reading stands behind 5:17, where Jesus says he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them.

Jewish teachers spoke of the yoke of the Torah and the yoke of the kingdom of heaven. Interpreters differ on how Jesus' yoke relates to them: many read it as the Torah as he interprets and fulfills it (5:17-20), others as his own person and teaching taking the Torah's central place. Either way, the yoke is received from a gentle teacher rather than imposed by heavy-handed ones (23:4).

Jesus reads the law by its purpose. Rules that guard holy things are good, yet Scripture itself shows that they yield to human need, and a reading of the law that forgets this has misunderstood the law's own story.

Jesus treats the written commandment as God's own speech and the elders' tradition as human, and he refuses to let the second overrule the first. He does not attack the law; he defends it against a practice that let people keep a rule while breaking a command.

How far this saying reaches is debated. Daniel Boyarin and others read it as a ruling about handwashing, the Pharisees' tradition, which leaves the Torah's food laws in place; Matthew's closing words in verse 20 support that reading. Others hold that the principle stated here is broader and that the church drew its full conclusion later, as Mark's comment (Mark 7:19) and Paul's conviction that nothing is unclean in itself (Romans 14:14) show. Both readings agree that Jesus moves the question of defilement from the hands to the heart.

Jesus measures defilement by the Ten Commandments rather than by rules of washing, which confirms that the moral law remains the standard of holiness in his teaching. By ending with handwashing (verse 20), Matthew limits the ruling to the question the Pharisees raised.

Jesus brings Israel's law of evidence into the life of his community. The procedure is not a way to multiply pressure on the accused but a safeguard of justice: no one is to be condemned on one person's word.

Jesus distinguishes within the law between what reveals God's design and what restrains human sin. The certificate was a real part of Moses' law, given by God, yet it was fitted to hard hearts; reading Deuteronomy through Genesis is how Jesus fulfills the law rather than abolishing it (5:17).

Jesus affirms the commandments as the way of life and joins them to the love command, so that the law's prohibitions are read as forms of love. Matthew's addition makes the man's claim in verse 20 a claim to have loved his neighbor as himself, which the call to give to the poor will test.

The double commandment does not abolish the other commandments; they hang on it. Every command is to be read as a form of love for God or neighbor, which is how Jesus has read the Sabbath and purity laws (12:1-14, 15:1-20). Paul says the same when he calls love the fulfillment of the Law (Romans 13:8-10).

Interpreters reconcile this verse with 16:12 in several ways. Mark Allan Powell (1995) argued that ‘Moses' seat’ refers to the scribes' role in reading the Torah aloud, so that Jesus commends what they read from Moses, not their own rulings. Others read ‘everything’ as limited to their faithful teaching of the Law, or take the command as ironic. On any reading, Jesus affirms the Law they teach and condemns the gap between their words and their lives, the same gap he warned of in 7:21-23.

The Law has an order of weight, and Jesus names it from the prophets: justice, mercy, and faithfulness echo Micah 6:8 and Hosea 6:6. Careful obedience in small things is commended, not dismissed; what is condemned is small obedience that becomes a substitute for the great.
Jesus does not bypass the law. He fulfills its purpose by making a man clean and then sends him to have that cleanness recognized according to the law.

Jesus interprets the law as its master, not as a rival rabbi. Christians have drawn different conclusions from this for Sunday worship and Sabbath keeping, but all agree the verse makes Jesus the one who defines the day's meaning.

Jesus distinguishes two authorities that his critics treated as one: the written command of God and the interpretive tradition built around it. He does not reject interpretation as such, but he insists that the command judges the tradition and never the reverse.

The verses show how a religious act can be turned into an escape from love of neighbor. Jesus reads the law by its weightier matters: a vow to God that injures one's parents fails the command it claims to honor.

For Mark, Jesus' teaching settles what the food laws were for: they marked Israel as holy, and the holiness they pointed to is a clean heart. The church read this as fulfillment rather than contempt, the law's intention met in Christ (compare Romans 14:14, Hebrews 9:10). Jewish readers such as Boyarin dispute that Jesus meant it so, which is why the grammar of this clause matters.

The verse distinguishes within the law between what reveals God's will and what restrains human sin. Some commands accommodate a fallen people to limit harm. Jesus does not set Moses aside; he reads one provision by the purpose of the Creator, a principle the church later used in distinguishing the law's abiding moral core from its concessions.
Jesus receives the sign of the Abrahamic covenant as every Jewish boy did. Paul's words that God's Son was ‘born of a woman, born under the law’ (Galatians 4:4) are narrated here.
The one who will fulfill the Law is first placed under it by his parents' obedience. Luke's repeated ‘according to the Law’ answers any suspicion that Jesus' movement began in disregard of Moses.
Jesus does not bypass the Law; he honors its procedures and sends the man to the priest. The Law declares clean; Jesus makes clean.

Jesus reads the Sabbath law by its purpose. A day given for rest and for remembering God's deliverance (Deuteronomy 5:15) is a fitting day for deliverance, and refusing to do good is not neutral obedience.

Jesus directs the lawyer to Scripture, not to a new teaching of his own. The two commands already stood in the Torah, and the verse shows Jesus upholding the Law's authority while he presses on its meaning.

Jesus does not lower the Law's demand to make it manageable. By answering in the Law's own words, he affirms that love for God and neighbor is the way of life, and the lawyer's next move (verse 29) shows how quickly the command becomes a matter for self-defense.
The command ends where verse 28 did, with doing. The parable does not replace the Law with a feeling; it shows what the Law's own command of love requires when it meets a wounded man on the road.

Jesus affirms tithing while condemning its misuse. He does not set the Law's small commands against its large ones, but orders them: faithfulness in detail is good only when it serves justice and love for God.

Interpreting the Law carries responsibility for how it lands on people. Jesus condemns teaching that multiplies obligations without helping anyone keep them, and invites the weary to a lighter yoke (Matthew 11:28-30); Peter makes the same objection to burdening Gentile believers (Acts 15:10).

Luke's Jesus affirms the Law's permanence in the strongest image available. How the Law continues is worked out in Luke-Acts: it is fulfilled in Christ (24:44), it still bears witness to him, and its intent is pressed deeper, as the next verse shows. The verse rules out reading the kingdom as the Law's cancellation.

Placed after verse 17, the saying shows what it means that no stroke of the Law will fail: its intent for marriage, stated at creation, is honored more strictly than the permissions the rabbis debated.

Jesus sends the ruler first to the Law, taking it seriously as God's word. The Law is not dismissed as a path to life; it is shown to be unfinished in this man, who has kept its outward commands and not yet given his heart.

The women rest ‘according to the commandment’ (Exodus 20:10). Luke portrays the first witnesses of the resurrection as faithful Jews who keep the Law even in grief, part of his larger case that the gospel is the fulfillment of Israel's faith, not a break from it.

The law is called a gift given through Moses, not a mistake corrected by Christ. The contrast is between a servant who delivered God's word and the Son in whom God's faithful love arrives in person, which is how John can later say that Moses wrote about Jesus (5:46).

The jars belong to the law's provision for purity, which was a gift for living near a holy God, not an empty form. John sets the sign exactly there, so that what the law's washings served is now surpassed in Jesus, as the prologue said: the law came through Moses, grace and truth through Jesus Christ (1:17).

Jesus appeals to the law against those who think they defend it. The law given through Moses forbids murder, and to plot the death of an innocent man in the name of the Sabbath law is to break the law one claims to guard, as 5:45-47 already warned.

The rulers use knowledge of the law to exclude and to curse, but they are about to be shown breaking it (7:51). The chapter turns the charge around: it is not the crowd's ignorance but the leaders' misuse of the law that stands under judgment.
Nicodemus's question shows that the law, rightly used, protects the accused. The rulers who pride themselves on knowing the law are rebuked from within it by one of their own.

The law is real and its penalty is real, and the scene does not pretend otherwise. What the passage exposes is the use of the law as an instrument: a person is set up as evidence in a case against someone else. The law given to protect the covenant community has become a trap.

Even without the written law, people know that God's just order condemns what they do. This is the knowledge Paul will call the law written on the heart (2:15), and it leaves every person answerable to God.

The law of Moses is the standard for those who have it, but it does not create accountability where it is absent. Gentiles are accountable for what they knew (1:20, 2:15), and Jews for what they were given.

Who are these Gentiles? One reading, found in Augustine's On the Spirit and the Letter and defended by Cranfield and Wright, sees Christian Gentiles in whom the new covenant promise of the law written on the heart has come true. Another, the older and still majority reading, sees pagans who at times do what the law requires, showing a moral knowledge that makes them accountable. Thomas Aquinas cited this verse as the scriptural warrant for natural law (Summa Theologiae I-II, question 91, article 2).

Teaching the law is not keeping it. Paul's questions apply the law's own commands to those who teach them, as Jesus did when he told the crowds to do what the scribes taught but not what they did (Matthew 23:3).

Who keeps the law's requirements while uncircumcised? As in verse 14, some see Christian Gentiles in whom the Spirit fulfills the law (8:4), and others a hypothetical case that sharpens the point. Paul's argument works either way: the sign without the reality is empty.

One purpose of the law is to silence self-justification. Before God's law, every human defense falls away, which the Reformation called the law's first use: to reveal sin and drive the sinner to seek grace.
The law is not evil, but it cannot justify; it brings knowledge of sin. Paul's later chapters show the law holy and good (7:12) yet powerless to give life because of the flesh (8:3).

Faith does not abolish God's law but upholds it. Justification apart from works of the law is not lawlessness; it is the fulfillment of what the law itself testified, and it produces the obedience the law could not.

The law works wrath because, meeting sinful people, it turns sin into conscious transgression and so exposes them to judgment. Paul will say in chapter 7 that the law is holy and good, yet it could not give life; its role is to reveal, not to rescue.

The law was never the solution; it entered to make sin's full extent visible. The Reformers called this its pedagogical use, driving people to grace. Paul will defend the law's goodness in chapter 7 while insisting it could not give life.

The verse implies that the law, good as it is, did not free anyone from sin's rule; chapter 7 will explain why. Christians have long disagreed over what ‘not under law’ means for the moral commands of the Old Testament: Reformed teaching distinguishes the law as a covenant of works, from which believers are freed, from the law as a rule of life, which still guides them; Lutheran teaching stresses the law's accusing role; many recent interpreters read ‘law’ here as the Mosaic covenant as an era of salvation history, now superseded in Christ.

The verse limits the law's jurisdiction to this life. Paul will argue that believers died with Christ (verse 4), so the law's claim as a regime over them has ended, though its holiness and goodness remain (verse 12).

Believers died ‘to the law’, not the law to them. The law is not abolished; the believer's relationship to it as a regime has ended through Christ's death, so that obedience now springs from belonging to Christ.

The law's first work here is revelation: it names sin for what it is. Paul does not say the law creates sin, but that without the command he would not have recognized his desire as sin. This is what Reformation theology called the law's second or theological use, to expose sin and drive the sinner to grace.

The strongest affirmation of the law in Paul's letters. Whatever Christians conclude about ‘not under law’, this verse forbids treating the law of Moses as defective or bad. The problem Paul diagnoses is sin, not Torah.

If nomos here is the law of Moses, Paul is saying that even with God's law in hand, evil stands ready. If it means a principle, he is naming a law of experience that competes with God's law. Either way, having God's law does not remove the problem.

The law's goal is reached, not abandoned. What the law required and could not produce through the flesh, the Spirit produces in those who belong to Christ, which is the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:27.

The law is good (Romans 7:12), but it cannot give life; it defines sin and so gives sin a legal power to condemn. Paul places the law on the side of the problem Christ solves, not because the law is evil but because sinners under it are condemned by it.

Paul calls the demand that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law a form of slavery. The law was not slavery in itself, but to require it of those who belong to Christ is to put them back under a guardian they have outgrown (3:23-25, 4:1-7).

Returning to the law as the condition of belonging undoes the gospel. Paul does not say the law was bad to have, but that to reinstate it as the dividing wall (compare Ephesians 2:14-15) contradicts what faith in Christ has already done.

The law blesses obedience and curses disobedience, and it demands complete obedience. Paul's point is that the law, taken as the ground of standing before God, cannot deliver the blessing it promises to people who do not keep it.

Paul contrasts the principle of the law (do and live) with the principle of faith (believe and live). The law's promise was real, but it rested on doing, and verse 10 has shown where that leaves those who fail to do.

The law had a real but limited purpose: it dealt with transgression and lasted until the seed came. Paul gives it a place in God's plan without allowing it to rival the promise, which came directly from God.
The law is not against the promises; it serves them by showing that no one can be made alive by keeping it. It was never God's instrument for giving life, which belongs to the Spirit.

The law's role was real but temporary, like a guardian's charge over a child. Luther drew from this passage the law's ‘theological use’, driving sinners to Christ by showing them their sin; Calvin added its role of restraining evil and guiding believers. Many modern interpreters emphasize instead the historical sense: the law governed Israel until the coming of Christ.

The law as a set of commandments separating Jew from Gentile no longer defines membership in God's people. Christian traditions explain the scope differently (the ceremonial law only, or the Mosaic covenant as a whole), but all agree the verse removes the law as a wall.

The Mosaic law and the Levitical priesthood stand together. The verse does not call the law evil; it says the law's priesthood could not bring the people to perfection, and Scripture itself (Psalm 110) looked beyond it.

The law and the priesthood cannot be separated. If the priest now comes from Judah, the arrangement of Sinai that tied priesthood to Levi has been set aside, and the law that governs God's people must be understood anew in light of the new priest.

‘The law made nothing perfect.’ The law could command and regulate, but it could not bring worshipers into God's presence with a clean conscience. Hebrews honors the law as God's gift while insisting that its purpose was preparatory.

The new covenant does not abolish God's law but relocates it, from stone tablets to human hearts. The obedience the old covenant commanded, the new one creates, which is how Ezekiel 36:26-27 describes the gift of the Spirit.
The food laws and washings were ‘imposed until the time of reform’. Hebrews treats them as temporary by design, which is how Mark 7:19 and Colossians 2:16-17 treat them as well.
The law is called a shadow cast by the good things to come. It pointed truly to Christ's work and so was not false, but it could not supply the reality it pictured.

The psalm's own words show that the sacrificial system was never God's final aim. The ‘first’ (the offerings of the law) gives way to the ‘second’ (the will of God done in obedience), a change made by God and announced in Israel's Scriptures.
